body_markdown:
About half a century ago or so, the first step in building a performance-oriented street rod or race car typically called for a trip to the local boneyard. Possibly you had already yanked the tired six-banger out of your project vehicle, and now you had to conjure up a potent power source as a replacement. The chances of finding a great engine ready to go were between zero and none unless you were willing to write a check with at least three of those zeroes, so what you were looking for was a good place to begin.


I recall searching for an engine for a clean but uninspired ’55 Chevy years ago. Making my way through a pile of motors that had been liberated from cars headed to the crusher, I eventually found a 327-cubic-inch[small-block](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/chevy-small-block-the-little-engine-that-did/) V-8 for the right price and hauled it home. Success! But only a complete teardown and rebuild could make it the kind of spirited engine the old Chevy deserved.


Today’s[horsepower-loving car guys and gals](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/engine-swap/) have it easier, although the price tag might be a big part of their budget. The answer may be “crate engines,” so called because yes, they do come in crates. They are factory-built and usually marketed by the original manufacturer; Ford, for instance, sells a ton of the 5.0-liter V-8 Coyote engines from the Mustang. Typically, OEM manufacturers don’t advertise crate engine prices, but aftermarket companies that stock crate engines might: Summit Racing, for instance, a well-known performance store, sells a Ford Performance Parts 5.0-liter, Gen 4X V-8 with an 80mm throttle body that pumps out 460 horsepower for $11,704.99. Prices may, and often do, vary considerably, especially since some versions include more parts than others.


Sure, you can build a magnificent engine from a good core with specialized aftermarket parts, or you can buy[a super motor from an engine builder](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/how-blueprint-engines-builds-80-crate-motors-a-day/) . But potent[crate engines](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/crate-engine/) in various levels of completion and in a wide range of sizes and horsepower ratings are now available from Chevrolet, Ford, Mopar and some aftermarket suppliers. For the average enthusiast, they’re often the best choice. Many of the crate offerings are more powerful than the maker’s production engines. In most cases both long-block and complete engines are available. (A long-block engine includes the assembled short block and complete cylinder heads, but other parts including intake, pumps and other external components are not included.) Complete engines are fully assembled and, for the most part, ready to run. Some come with a parts warranty; check the manufacturers’ websites for warranty details before you sign on the dotted line.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


In the sections that follow, you will notice that we list the displacement of some engines in liters, while others are in cubic inches. In all cases, we followed the lead of the manufacturers; some use the metric displacement figure for newer products, and a standard cubic-inch figure for classic stuff. Horsepower and torque numbers are for reference only and are no guarantee that the cited output can be achieved in a given application.


Installing a crate engine in a late-model vehicle may not be legal in all jurisdictions. Stellantis, for example, warns that its crate Hemi engines ae designed for installation in motor vehicles manufactured prior to model year 1976 or in competition vehicles driven on tracks or off road. And they of course note that the customer is responsible for compliance. Other manufacturers offer similar warnings.


Let’s take a look at some powerplants currently available from the Detroit three:


## Chevrolet


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Chevrolet offers approximately 35 different crate engines through their performance dealer network. The offerings include powerplants based on LS, LSX and LT production engines, along with traditional small-block 350- and 383-cubic-inch powerplants, a few re-engineered big-block variants and even some sealed race engines for spec racing. All of the crate engines and some other performance parts can be seen on the Chevrolet Performance[website](https://www.chevrolet.com/performance-parts/crate-engines?ppc=GOOGLE_5153940642_19598269191_145066335546_&d_src=313715&d_adsrc=3876783&d_campaign=19598269191&d_site=GOOGLE&d_adgroup=145066335546&d_keyword=&gclick=CjwKCAjw4dDTBhAqEiwAkHYmStzg1MN_IK5mMSo1qswErNxePJWirdHgCPlNb8rZf9rHXSbGCuBB1xoC0VgQAvD_BwE&gclsrc=aw.ds&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=19598269191&gbraid=0AAAAADf3ZAAKBYA-wxGU-sEPkAwcv-oAP&gclid=CjwKCAjw4dDTBhAqEiwAkHYmStzg1MN_IK5mMSo1qswErNxePJWirdHgCPlNb8rZf9rHXSbGCuBB1xoC0VgQAvD_BwE) . None of the crate engines are pure production engines. Many have been modified for higher performance and were chosen for the program because they lend themselves well to performance upgrades.


Most Chevy crate engines can be purchased as part of a package that includes the engine, engine controller, transmission, transmission installation kit, torque converter and transmission control system, where applicable. These packages make the task of installing a modern powertrain in a street rod or classic car a true plug-and-play task. Chevy Performance crate engines and packages can only be purchased through Chevy dealers that are designated Chevrolet Performance Centers. There are approximately 80 such dealers in the U.S. Should a customer need help with an application, the dealers are equipped with flow charts that enable them to resolve some issues.


Some aftermarket companies offer Chevrolet crate engines as well. But according to GM sources, all were originally purchased through a Chevrolet Performance Center. That’s not to say that a Chevy crate engine purchased from an aftermarket speed equipment supplier is inferior. In fact, the seller may package it with upgrades and other equipment. But, according to GM, the original source of the engine is a Chevrolet Performance Center.


Blake Nye was a key player in Chevy Performance’s crate engine program. For[his own 1950 GMC restomod](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/engineer-takes-50-gmc-pickup-from-stovebolt-to-stylin/) , he chose an LS3 engine with LS9 CNC-ported cylinder heads, all from Chevrolet Performance. The engine control system is from Chevrolet Performance.


Paul Stenquist


In a telephone interview, retired GM engineer Blake Nye and Design Release Engineer Roderick Payne filled us in on the potentially confusing world of GM performance engine names. First, it’s important to note that while the designations LS, LT and others are a handy way to establish categories, they are relatively meaningless. They don’t describe a hierarchy or even a chronological production order. They are simply manufacturing designations originally meant for internal use. We use them here because they at least provide some way of organizing the Chevrolet Performance Center crate engine offerings.


**The LT engine group** includes three engines all of which are pushrod engines and are equipped with direct fuel injection. The L8P can be ordered with up to 523 horsepower and 543 lb-ft of torque from 6.6 liters of displacement. The L8T, which is based on an HD truck engine, offers up to 401 horsepower and 464 lb-ft of torque from 6.6 liters. The LT4 is offered with up to 650 horsepower and 650 lb-ft of torque from 6.2 liters. The LT1 comes with up to 455 horsepower and 455 lb-ft of torque from 6.2 liters of displacement


The Chevrolet LS3 crate engine is based on the C6 Corvette engine of the same name but has been updated. It’s offered in versions up to 6.2 liters and 525 horsepower and is the brand’s best-selling crate engine.


GM


**The LS/LSX engine group** includes three offerings, which are meant to be carbureted or fitted with external fuel injection. The LS3, developed from the C6 Corvette engine of the same name, is available with up to 525 horsepower and 486 lb-ft of torque in displacements up to 6.2 liters. It’s currently the most popular choice for Chevrolet engine swaps. The LS9 long block is capable of generating up to 638 horsepower and 604 lb-ft of torque from 6.2 liters of displacement. The LSX long-block engine can be ordered in a trim that is capable of up to 627 horsepower and 586 lb-ft of torque from as much as 7.4 liters. It features six head bolts per cylinder for optimum clamping. The LSX was never offered in a production car but was developed as a heavy-duty, high-performance crate engine. Its stout iron block is said to be able to support up to 2000 horsepower. It’s offered in two displacements: 454 or 376 cubic inches.


The 454-cubic-inch version of the LSX small-block Chevrolet engine. Its cylinder block and head clamping are said to be stout enough to handle 2000 horsepower.


GM


**The Small-Block engine group** includes two offerings named by their cubic inches, called the 350 and the 383 families. Both are available in a variety of configurations and come with dual-plane aluminum intake manifolds that mount a single four-barrel carb or electronic fuel injection. These first-generation small-blocks are great for applications where a traditional look is desirable. The 350 can be equipped to produce up to 420 horsepower and 408 lb-ft of torque in displacements up to 5.7 liters. The 383 can produce up to 450 horsepower and 436 lb-ft of torque in displacements up to 6.3 liters.


**The Big-Block Engine group** includes four offerings, ranging from a 427-cubic-inch version that is available with up to 480 horsepower, to the 632-cubic-inch monster with up to 1004 horsepower.


The 632-cubic-inch Chevrolet big-block is offered in a version that produces more than 1000 horsepower.


GM


**The Racing Engine Group** includes three factory-sealed competition crate engines meant for spec racing.


While complete plug-and-play options are a great choice for many, Chevrolet offers a full range of engine components as well. The 2026 Chevrolet Performance catalog lists them by category. For example, the LS, LT and LSX components comprise one section of the catalog, while small-block and big-block components have their own sections. In all, the catalog includes over 200 pages of performance goodies, along with a list of the Chevrolet Performance Dealers authorized to sell crate engines and performance components. Offerings include blocks, both fully machined and otherwise; cylinder heads of various configurations—including some with CNC-machined ports—plus rocker arms, gaskets, valves, pushrods, accessory drive kits and more. You can purchase a hard copy of the catalog at[Chevyperformancecatalog.com](https://chevyperformancecatalog.com/) ($9.95). A digital version can be downloaded or viewed at Chevrolet .com.


## Ford


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


On its performance parts[website](https://performanceparts.ford.com/engines/) , Ford offers approximately 23 different crate engines in a wide variety of categories ranging from the esteemed Coyote powerplants right down to an Ecoboost 2.3-liter 4-banger. Some of the engines in the Coyote and 7.3-liter group can be packaged with transmissions. Wiring and control modules are also available for some engines. Components are available as well, including crankshafts, cams, heads, cylinder blocks and more. Ford does not offer a printed catalog but all offerings can be found online. Ford crate engines and performance parts can be purchased through any Ford dealer and from aftermarket suppliers.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


**Ford’s Coyote Engine Group** includes five offerings ranging from the 460-horsepower, 420-lb-ft 5.0-liter powerplant with a single throttle body, up to a supercharged 760-horsepower, 625-lb-ft 5.2-liter monster motor with CNC-ported aluminum heads and a supercharger.


Mike Goodwin, a product manager for Ford Performance, says the 5.0-liter Gen 4X Coyote is Ford’s best-selling crate engine. The 32-valve DOHC V-8 is conservatively rated at 460 horsepower, but is said to be capable of much more. According to Goodwin, “It’s actually closer to 480 horsepower as sold, so if the customer puts it on a dyno, they’ll be delighted to see how much power it actually makes.”


Ford’s 363-cubic-inch, 507-horsepower Boss crate engine is based on the automaker’s 302 small-block architecture.


Ford


**The 302 Group** includes at least five engines including a 302-cubic-inch V-8 with 340 horsepower and 350 lb-ft of torque; it has a cast iron block with aluminum heads. And there’s a 363-cubic-inch, 507-horse V-8 with a cast-iron long-block and with aluminum Z2 heads; it’s is the top seller in this group. These pushrod, cam-in-block engines are based on heritage 302 small-block architecture. They’re now built with all-new parts and castings and are said to be vastly superior to the original designs.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


**The** **Race Engine Group** includes three factory-sealed engines for spec racing series. All are 347-cubic-inches and are based on the Boss 302 architecture. Two generate 415 horsepower, and a third is 350 horses.


Ford’s 572-cubic-inch, 655-horsepower big-block crate engine is based on the 460/429 architecture.


Ford


**The** **Big-Block Group** offers two 572-cubic-inch monsters, both capable of producing 655 horsepower and 710 lb-ft of torque. These stout powerplants are based on the venerable 460-cubic-inch engine that first saw service in Lincolns. Other engines in this architecture family include the 429 Cobra Jet and Super Cobra Jet.


**The 351 Group** includes two 427-cubic-inch engines that are capable of generating 535 horsepower and 545 lb-ft of torque, and two 460-cubic-inch, 575-horsepower versions that can produce 575 lb-ft of torque. These are small-block engines based on the Boss 351. While dimensionally compact, they offer huge performance.


Ford displayed a 430-horsepower, 7.3-liter “Godzilla” crate engine in a 1966 Galaxie convertible at Metro Detroit’s Woodward Dream Cruise. The engine was packaged with Ford’s 10R80 transmission, electronic control unit and low-profile manifold. It’s a plug and play installation.


Said Deep


**The 7.3L Group** includes two big-displacement “Godzilla” engines. These are based on Ford’s Super Duty truck engine and can be tuned to produce massive horsepower. They are very popular in swaps because they’re dimensionally more compact than Coyote engines and can even fit in the venerable Fox-body Mustang. One of the crate offerings is said to be capable of generating 430 horsepower and 485 lb-ft of torque; the other can produce 612 horsepower and 670 lb-ft of torque.


**An Ecoboost V-6** generates 290 horsepower from 3.3 liters, while a **2.3-liter Ecoboost 4-cylinder** knocks out 310 horsepower.


## Mopar


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Mopar is a division of Stellantis, and it provides performance parts for Dodge, Ram, Jeep and Chrysler, with the emphasis on Dodge and Ram. Mopar shows nine crate engine offerings on its[website](https://www.dcperformance.com/crate-power/crate-engine) , most of which are versions of the company’s Generation III Hemi V-8. Production versions of this engine have been used in Stellantis brands for more than 30 years.


Mopar’s Helliphant crate engine is a supercharged GEN 3 Hemi that can generate 1025 horsepower and 945 lb-ft- of torque from 7.0 liters of displacement.


Stellantis


**Hemi V-8 Engine** offerings range from a long-block version of the 345-cubic-inch Hemi, which produced 383 horsepower and 417 lb-ft of torque in 2015-and-up Dodge Challengers, to a 1025-horsepower Hellephant 6.2-liter supercharged Hemi that knocks out 945 lb-ft of torque. This engine is obviously a cylinder-pressure beast, and Stellantis recommends E85 fuel. The Mopar web page says, “This is your chance to have the heart of the world’s most powerful muscle car ever built.” A 6.2-liter Hellcrate Hemi long block is available as well at a much lower price. This offering is said to be capable of 717 horsepower and 656 lb-ft of torque when properly equipped. A 392 Crate Hemi long block is said to be capable of 485 horsepower and 475 lb-ft torque.


The Cat 3 Hurricrate inline 6-cylinder is capable of 550 horsepower and 531 lb-ft of torque.


Stellantis


**Inline-6 Cylinder Engines** are now a vital part of the Stellantis high-performance lineup, and several crate engine versions are available. The Cat 1 Hurricrate twin-turbo, 183-cubic-inch inline 6-cylinder can deliver up to 420 horsepower and 468 lb-ft of torque. The Cat 3 version pumps out 550 horsepower and 531 lb-ft of torque. Both complete and long block versions of the engine are available. Talk about street sleepers: “Hey, gimme a two-car head start; it’s just a six!”
